desc:
The array nums has an even length. Split its elements into pairs so that every element is in exactly one pair. The pair sum of a pair is the sum of its two elements.

Among all ways to form the pairs, return the smallest possible value of the largest pair sum.

For example, [3, 5, 2, 3] gives 7: pairing (3, 3) and (5, 2) gives sums 6 and 7, and no pairing can keep both below 7. For [1, 1, 9, 9] the answer is 10.
hints: Try pairing the largest element with something. What partner keeps its sum as small as possible?
The largest element should be paired with the smallest element; otherwise some smaller partner would make a sum that is at least as bad for the large one.
Sort, then pair s[i] with s[n-1-i] for every i, and return the largest of these sums.
editorial: Exchange argument: let big be the largest element and small the smallest. Suppose an optimal pairing has big with some x and small with some y. Swapping partners gives pairs (big, small) and (x, y). Since small ≤ x we get big + small ≤ big + x, and since y ≤ big we get x + y ≤ x + big, so neither new sum exceeds the old maximum. Repeating the argument on the remaining elements shows the greedy pairing is optimal.
So sort and pair from both ends, tracking the maximum sum. This is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the pairing.
